papers.title: Differentially Private Manifold Denoising
papers.abstract: Modern data analysis increasingly relies on manifold-based methods that use local geometry to extract low-dimensional structure from noisy observations. Yet in domains such as biomedicine and public health, privacy regulations restrict access to individual-level data, while perturbations introduced to protect privacy can distort the geometric information needed for analysis. We introduce a manifold denoising framework that uses private reference data to correct noisy public queries, bringing differential privacy to local geometric estimation. Starting from a hard correction based on the estimated tangent space, we develop a noise-adaptive soft correction that avoids specifying the intrinsic dimension. Furthermore, we construct a shared Gaussian field that couples evaluations across locations and bandwidths with moderate marginal noise inflation. Under standard assumptions on manifold regularity and sampling density, we establish non-asymptotic utility guarantees that characterize how denoising accuracy depends on sample size, noise level, bandwidth, and the privacy budget. Simulations and UK Biobank applications demonstrate accurate signal recovery under moderate privacy budgets. These results illustrate clear utility--privacy trade-offs and provide a practical DP component for manifold-based workflows in regulated environments.

papers.title: Pathwise Factorization and Uncertainty Quantification for Impedance Obstacles with Random Boundaries
papers.abstract: We develop a factorization method with finite-sample statistical guarantees for two-dimensional acoustic scattering by impedance obstacles whose boundary is random and whose data are finitely many noisy multistatic measurements. In the two-dimensional far-field normalization, the symmetrization must act on a phase-rotated far-field operator; we prove the optical and range identities for every realization of a compact family of uniformly bi-Lipschitz domains, with jointly measurable regularized indicators. A quadrature-weighted finite-sample analysis separates angular approximation, measurement noise, test-vector error, and regularization, and yields a consistency theorem for empirical means and variances, joint in all data parameters. Bounded indicators admit simultaneous confidence bands, a diagonal threshold recovers the probability that a sampling point lies in the random obstacle, and a nested design yields unbiased variance components. Computations use a combined-field integral equation proved invertible at all frequencies, and the finite-grid guarantees are examined in a coverage study against a high-accuracy Monte Carlo reference.

papers.title: Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?
papers.abstract: Semiparametric models provide a broad framework for statistical inference, yet efficient estimation typically relies on influence function correction tailored to each estimand and on nuisance estimation repeated for every sample. We show that a single pretrained Transformer can deliver efficient estimation and valid inference for a family of estimands in one forward pass, without deriving efficient influence functions or estimating nuisance functions. Pretrained on simulated data with the true parameter as the only label, the Transformer learns the posterior mean and covariance of the queried estimand and hence returns an estimate and a Wald-type confidence region. Theoretically, we prove that, for locally flat pretraining priors of slowly growing complexity, the posterior mean is efficient for every queried estimand. The Transformer inherits this efficiency with asymptotically exact coverage, in probability over evaluation populations and queries, even under distribution shift. We also reveal that the guarantee places much higher demands on pretraining when the data-generating distribution is fixed, as in classical frequentist inference. Experiments on causal inference, partial linear regression, and survival analysis show that the pretrained model generally achieves the lowest estimation error among competing methods, with nearly nominal coverage, at a computational cost of only about 0.02 seconds per dataset.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs
papers.abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich health information for uncovering latent patient representations and clinically meaningful subgroups. Learning from EHR data across institutions is valuable because representations learned at a single site may reflect local data patterns and lack generalizability, yet pooling patient-level records across institutions is often impractical because of privacy constraints and communication costs. We propose a communication-efficient, non-iterative federated spectral method for learning shared latent representation components from multi-institutional EHRs, in which each institution shares aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary while keeping patient-level records local. A central server aggregates these summaries with the pooled marginal frequencies to recover both the shared low-rank structure and the canonical row-normalization direction required for interpretable representation recovery. We prove row-wise recovery guarantees and error bounds, with a leading federated variance term matching a corresponding lower bound under explicit regularity conditions. Simulations show that our method closely matches pooled analysis in estimating latent representation components, improves as more sites contribute summaries, and outperforms single-site and existing federated benchmarks across a range of data settings. Applied to real-world multi-facility EHR data for stroke patients, the method learns interpretable patient representations that highlight clinically distinct subgroups and could help inform subgroup-specific care.

papers.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts
papers.abstract: Reweighting source samples to match a target covariate distribution is a standard response to distribution shift when generalizing evidence across populations. It is well suited to deterministic, learnable covariate discrepancies, but can fail when source--target differences extend beyond covariate shift or when estimation of the density-ratio weights is unstable. We introduce a new model where the discrepancy between two population laws comprises a deterministic covariate shift and a non-systematic component, modeled as random perturbation of the probability space. This separates systematic shifts, treated as bias and corrected by reweighting, from random perturbations, treated as distributional uncertainty and reduced by dataset pooling. Under pure random perturbations, this principle yields Augmented Inverse Distance Weighting, which combines regression augmentation with variance-optimal dataset-level pooling and attains asymptotic variance no larger than exact covariate balancing. When both components are present, we develop Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting, which interpolates between AIDW and standard augmented importance weighting. Both estimators tradeoff sampling and distributional uncertainty via a distributional distance quantifying the strength of random perturbations. We establish asymptotic normality of both estimators and provide tuning and diagnostic tools. On three real-world multi-site datasets exhibiting diverse distribution shifts, the proposed methods consistently reduce mean-squared error compared with weighting baselines, and improve empirical coverage when covariate-shift adjustment alone undercovers.

papers.title: A Dynamical Theory of LoRA in Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Despite the widespread use of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), little is known about its dynamics in continual learning and the mechanisms by which low-rank updates affect catastrophic forgetting. We provide an asymptotically exact dynamical characterization of LoRA in a solvable two-task teacher-student model. In the high-dimensional online-learning limit, we derive a closed system of ordinary differential equations for a finite set of macroscopic order parameters, yielding exact expressions for the generalization errors throughout both the initial Task 1 learning phase and the subsequent LoRA fine-tuning on Task 2. The theory quantitatively matches finite-dimensional simulations and exposes two characteristic effects of LoRA: when the first-task representation is not yet specialized, low-rank adaptation reduces interference with features learned on the first task, but its initialization slows adaptation to the second task. Building on this mechanistic picture, we analyze a state-dependent masking strategy that freezes hidden units carrying the strongest first-task representations and restricts adaptation to the complementary subspace. This structural partitioning markedly reduces forgetting, while preserving plasticity on the new task. Our framework further clarifies the role of adapter rank: transfer improves only up to the intrinsic dimensionality of the target task and saturates beyond it, while forgetting continues to grow with rank. These results provide a dynamical and geometric account of how low-rank adaptation organizes information across sequential tasks, and are qualitatively reproduced on sequential MNIST and CIFAR-100 using a shallow network and ResNet-18, respectively.

papers.title: A functional Breuer-Major theorem under finite variance, with application to the $R/S$ test for long memory
papers.abstract: The Breuer-Major theorem (Breuer and Major, 1983) states that, for a function $G$ of Hermite rank $m$ such that $\mathbb{E}(G^{2}(X))<\infty$, and a stationary Gaussian sequence whose correlation function $r$ satisfies $\sum_{i}|r(i)|^{m}<\infty$, the finite dimensional distributions of the normalized partial sum process of $G(X_{i})$ converge to those of a Brownian motion. Whether the functional version of this result holds under these sole conditions has remained open for a long time, the tightness being known only under additional moment assumptions. In this paper we prove that the functional central limit theorem holds under finite variance only. More generally, we give a high order expansion of the partial sum process which covers both short and long-range dependence: the long-range dependent components converge to Hermite processes, while the remainder converges to a Brownian motion. As an application, we discuss the question of testing long-memory in observed data using the $R/S$ statistics. We derive the limiting distributions of the classical and modified $R/S$ statistics, prove the consistency of the test and propose a data-driven choice of the truncation parameter. A Monte Carlo study compares the performances of the classical and modified $R/S$ statistics for both short-memory and long-memory sequences.

papers.title: On the Role of Fisher Information, Variance and Asymptotics in Statistical Inference
papers.abstract: Bahadur's \emph{Lectures on the Theory of Estimation} close with a chapter on asymptotics: asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, Fisher's bound on its asymptotic variance with Hodges's counterexample, and local asymptotic normality. A companion paper read the earlier lectures with one modification, replacing the point estimator by a generalized estimator---Fisher's continuum of significance tests---assessed by information rather than variance. This paper reads Chapter 8 the same way. At each of its three parts the classical statement is an approximation about a point estimator, while the corresponding statement about the score is exact at every sample size. Superefficiency does not arise, because information is bounded by the Fisher information at every $n$; Hodges's estimator, computed exactly, is fully efficient at the origin and loses information only where its mean square error is worst. The information of a generalized estimator is argued to be Fisher information: the mean rate at which a continuum of tests responds to the parameter, standardized by its variance. The resulting Fisher upper bound differs geometrically, not merely algebraically, from the Cram\'er--Rao lower bound. The extension is not empty: the $t$-test continuum loses about half an observation's worth of the information in $\bar X$ at every $n$.

papers.title: An Asymptotic One-Sample Surrogate for Non-Gaussian ERM with General Convex Regularization
papers.abstract: We study convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) with non-Gaussian features and nonsmooth penalties through a surrogate driven by a single Gaussian vector. The surrogate preserves the penalty and calibrates its coefficients using the actual joint law of the feature-label model. We prove that this population calibration exists and is unique. We prove a Gaussian approximation for fresh prediction scores when the data satisfy a Poincar\'e inequality. Together with regularity conditions on the losses, this approximation yields agreement between the ERM minimizer and its surrogate in normalized means and prediction variances, as well as formulas for prediction and classification risks. The result covers general uniformly strongly convex penalties and pure Lasso under projection anti-concentration. The core proof relies on a cavity Hamilton-Jacobi argument that compares the main statistics of the two minimizers without differentiating the penalty.

papers.title: A sharp dimension barrier for uniform Gaussian approximations
papers.abstract: We establish a universal dimension barrier for Gaussian approximations based on $n$ i.i.d. random vectors $X_1,...,X_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Fix $m\in(2,\infty)$ and consider mean-zero distributions with coordinate variances bounded from below by a fixed positive constant and coordinatewise $m$th absolute moments bounded from above by a fixed constant. We show that \begin{equation*} \log d=o\left(n^{(m-2)/(3m-2)}\right) \end{equation*} is necessary for any sequence of statistics to admit a Gaussian approximation to its distribution uniformly over this distribution class and all hyperrectangles. Here, the centered Gaussian target is required to have the covariance or correlation matrix of the observations. The obstruction includes randomized procedures and already holds for coordinate maxima. Conversely, for $m\in(2,4]$, we establish that this growth condition on $d$ is sufficient for the distribution of a vector of centered and scaled quantile-winsorized means to obey a Gaussian approximation with covariance target without further restrictions on the covariances of the observations or knowledge of $m$. Thus, the dimension barrier is sharp in this moment range. For $m\in(4,\infty)$, the same statistic attains the barrier up to a power of $\log n$.

papers.title: Estimating contextual networks via Fisher-scoring surrogate likelihood
papers.abstract: When networks are accompanied by vertex-level covariates, effectively integrating and aligning the information underlying both data sources becomes a natural yet critical task. Current spectral approaches, despite their popularity, may yield suboptimal results and necessitate the specification of additional tuning parameters that are contingent upon unobservable signal-to-noise ratios. We propose a tuning-free, likelihood-based learning framework for estimating latent positions in contextual generalized random dot product graphs in the presence of high-dimensional vertex covariates with a low-rank structure. Our method constructs a smooth surrogate likelihood and implements a Fisher-scoring algorithm to iteratively estimate latent positions without introducing additional tuning parameters that depend on the network sparsity. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the Fisher-scoring estimator. Application to real-world data further demonstrates the method's practical utility, offering a principled and scalable alternative to spectral approaches for analyzing contextual networks in high-dimensional settings.

papers.title: Estimating conditional means under missingness-not-at-random with incomplete auxiliary variables
papers.abstract: Estimators assuming missingness at random (MAR) can fail under missingness not at random (MNAR). Introducing complete auxiliary variables sometimes restores MAR by breaking dependence between analysis variables and missingness. However, if the auxiliaries are themselves incomplete, MAR typically remains violated. We derive necessary and sufficient, weaker-than-MAR conditions under which the MAR functional $\mu_{\rm MAR}$ for a conditional mean $E[Y \mid X]$ is correct. We also propose an alternative identifying functional for $E[Y \mid X]$, called $\mu_{\rm MIA}$ for "Marginalization over Incomplete Auxiliaries", along with sufficient conditions for $\mu_{\rm MIA}$ to be correct. For MNAR distributions in which all missingness patterns can occur and certain context-specific independences do not occur, there are two straightforward cases where $\mu_{\rm MIA}$ is correct for a strict superset of the MNAR distributions for which $\mu_{\rm MAR}$ is correct: (1) $X$ is complete and $Y$ is incomplete; or (2) all auxiliary variables are incomplete. In case (1), $\mu_{\rm MAR}$ is always incorrect, barring knife-edge cases. Determining whether either case holds requires no knowledge of the MNAR mechanism. We propose estimators of $\mu_{\rm MIA}$, including g-computation and doubly robust estimators. Our R package miapack implements a semiparametric iterated-conditional-expectations estimator. We illustrate with real data and present simulations comparing estimators of $\mu_{\rm MIA}$ and $\mu_{\rm MAR}$.

papers.title: Subspace Inference for Multilayer Latent Space Networks: Intrinsic Geometry and One-Step Estimator
papers.abstract: Multilayer networks on a common node set, such as brain connectomes of several animals with one layer per animal, often share a low-dimensional geometry but differ in how strongly each layer expresses it and in node activity. We study a multilayer latent space network model that combines an invariant subspace common to all layers with layer-specific interaction matrices and node-by-layer degree effects. By introducing the generalized Cayley transform of the invariant subspace, we characterize the intrinsic geometry of the model and obtain sharp convergence rates for the maximum likelihood estimator, asymptotic normality and Neyman orthogonality for vertex-level parameters, and asymptotic normality for the interaction matrices with a non-negligible bias. Plug-in estimates of the bias and covariance give debiased confidence regions and tests of equality between layers. We also propose an easy-to-implement one-step estimator that attains the same vertex-level limits. In a real-world mouse connectome dataset, the inbred strain that lacks a corpus callosum shows about twice the hemispheric segregation of the other three strains.

papers.title: Smoothed Conformal Testing with Small Calibration Sets
papers.abstract: A small calibration sample restricts split conformal $p$-values to a coarse rank grid. Randomization removes this discretization, but its effect depends on both the smoothing interval and the allocation of auxiliary random variables. Independent tie-block randomization is exactly valid under null exchangeability. When calibration and null scores are jointly exchangeable conditional on the alternative scores, we prove positive regression dependence and hence Benjamini--Hochberg false discovery rate control, including for atomic score distributions. Smoothing over calibration-dependent rank cells agrees with tie-block randomization when calibration scores are distinct and no test score ties a calibration score, but can fail marginal validity with atoms. Assigning sorted random draws according to score order can invalidate even a single null $p$-value. An exact two-test example violates the usual $\pi_0\alpha$ bound, and simulations with continuous scores exhibit false discovery rates above the nominal level $\alpha$. Finally, conditional moment identities and normal-model illustrations show that removing the rank grid does not remove calibration uncertainty. Randomization can produce additional discoveries, including when ordinary conformal testing cannot reject at all, but it does not generally substitute for a larger calibration sample.

papers.title: Adaptive Redescending Regression with $q$-Polynomial Losses
papers.abstract: We introduce a family of smooth $q$-polynomial losses for robust joint regression--scale estimation. The family contains the Cauchy loss at $q=1$ and converges pointwise to the squared loss as $q$ increases. For every finite $q$, its regression score is bounded and redescending, while its scale score is bounded and permits explicit analysis of scale existence. We formulate simultaneous estimation through a surrogate likelihood with a common scale calibration $\kappa=1/2$ and select $q$ by maximizing the normalized surrogate likelihood over a finite candidate set. We investigate existence, large-sample behaviour, and the robustness implications of the loss family and discuss how optional modification of the scale score, for example by taking $\kappa=q/2$, can increase the threshold against scale explosion. This breakdown-oriented adjustment is distinct from the baseline estimator and requires its own joint breakdown analysis. An MM-type algorithm provides a practical implementation. Numerical investigations assess the resulting robustness--efficiency trade-off under different tail regimes.

papers.title: On min-Storey estimators for multiple testing and conformal novelty detection
papers.abstract: In a multiple testing task, finding an appropriate estimator of the proportion $\pi_0$ of non-signal in the data to boost power of false discovery rate (FDR) controlling procedures is a long-standing research theme, sometimes referred to as 'adaptive FDR control'. The interest in this theme has been reinforced in the recent years with conformal novelty detection, for which it turns out that similar tools can be used in combination with any 'blackbox' machine learning algorithm. Nevertheless, perhaps surprisingly, finding a solution for 'adaptive FDR control' that is optimal in a broad sense is still an open problem. This paper fills this gap by introducing new $\pi_0$-estimators, referred to as min-Storey (MS) and interval-min-Storey (IMS), which are built upon the so-called 'Storey estimator'. Plugging these estimators in the adaptive Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is shown to deliver FDR control both in the independent and conformal settings. In addition, these methods satisfy an optimal power property over any (regular) alternative distribution. The excellent behaviors of the new adaptive procedures are illustrated with numerical experiments both in the independent and conformal models for various distribution structures.

papers.title: Random weighting inference for linear regression under serial dependence of unknown form
papers.abstract: We construct confidence regions for a linear regression's coefficients, with regressors and errors forming a stationary ergodic sequence of serial dependence not necessarily known. We weight the observations by random variables from an independent auxiliary sample and estimate the coefficients by weighted least squares. We prove the estimator to be asymptotically normal with the sandwich covariance if and only if the bandwidth shrinks fast enough for the weights' randomness to dominate the score's serial dependence. Wald regions have the nominal level, under short memory with the dependence left unspecified and under long memory with a non-normal least-squares limit. We derive a condition specific to the slopes and a bandwidth from consistent memory-order estimates, and identify the estimator asymptotically with least squares perturbed by independent noise. In simulations, we compare our regions with self-normalized, fixed-bandwidth, and resampled intervals under short and long memory, and we apply the method to daily wind speeds at Irish stations, a long-memory series.

papers.title: The Sample Complexity of Distributed Simple Binary Hypothesis Testing under Information Constraints
papers.abstract: This paper resolves two open problems from a recent paper, arXiv:2403.16981, concerning the sample complexity of distributed simple binary hypothesis testing under information constraints. The first open problem asks whether interaction reduces the sample complexity of distributed simple binary hypothesis testing. In this paper, we show that sequential interaction does not help. The second problem suggests tightening existing sample complexity bounds for communication-constrained simple binary hypothesis testing. We derive optimally tight bounds for this setting and resolve this problem. Our main technical contributions are: (i) a one-shot lower bound on the Bayes error in simple binary hypothesis testing that satisfies a crucial tensorisation property; (ii) a streamlined proof of the formula for the sample complexity of simple binary hypothesis testing without constraints, first established in arXiv:2403.16981; and (iii) a reverse data-processing inequality for Hellinger-$\lambda$ divergences, generalising the results from arXiv:1812.03031 and arXiv:2206.02765.

papers.title: Efficient Inference for Inverse Reinforcement Learning and Dynamic Discrete Choice Models
papers.abstract: In many sequential decision-making problems, researchers observe actions but not the rewards that drive behavior, yet wish to evaluate counterfactual policies. Flexible inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods accommodate rich reward representations but typically lack valid inference, whereas classical dynamic discrete choice (DDC) methods provide inference under restrictive parametric structure. We develop a semiparametric framework for debiased inverse reinforcement learning in maximum-entropy IRL and Gumbel-shock DDC models. We show that the log behavior policy acts as a pseudo-reward, identifying policy-value differences without point identifying the reward and, under a normalization, yielding a point-identified reward representative. This reduces inference on reward-dependent estimands to inference on smooth functionals of the behavior policy and transition kernel. We establish pathwise differentiability and characterize efficient influence functions through reward and transition Riesz representers, with the transition component obtainable from existing observed-reward off-policy evaluation theory. For normalized rewards, we derive an explicit transformation of these representers that accounts for the normalization constraint. We construct automatic debiased machine-learning estimators that permit flexible nuisance estimation while attaining $\sqrt{n}$-consistency, asymptotic normality, and semiparametric efficiency. We illustrate the theory through efficient inference for fixed-policy values under pseudo-rewards and normalized rewards, and for counterfactual values when the agent reoptimizes over a restricted action set.

papers.title: Interval Inverse Inequalities for Multiscale Kernel Primitives with Positive Exponential Spectra
papers.abstract: Inverse inequalities are fundamental for controlling derivative growth and ensuring sampling stability in kernel-based approximation. Extending whole-space and single-scale estimates to multiscale analytic spaces on bounded intervals requires uniform control of boundary truncation and cross-scale cancellation. We establish unweighted $L^2(0,1)$ inverse inequalities of sharp scaling order $h_*^{-1}$ for trial spaces spanned by affine functions and multiscale primitives of kernels with positive exponential spectra, where $h_*$ denotes the finest scale. Under geometric scale separation and within-scale center separation, the inverse constant depends only on the kernel and separation parameters; it is independent of the number of scales and centers, allowing centers at the endpoints and arbitrary cross-scale center coincidences. To prove the bound, we combine an exterior Gram decomposition with endpoint-distance weights to establish configuration-uniform Riesz bounds for normalized high-order derivatives of order $q$, whose lower constant approaches the optimal limit $1/2$. A synthesis-operator perturbation argument and parameterized interval interpolation then yield the first-order estimate. Two-center constructions confirm sharpness in both the scaling order $h_*^{-1}$ and the $q^{-1/2}$ asymptotic deficit from $1/2$ as $q \to \infty$. An application to deterministic least-squares sampling is derived, and numerical experiments on boundary-layer asymptotics, multiscale Gram spectra, sharp inverse constants, and midpoint sampling illustrate the theory.

papers.title: Improved Constants in the Kautz-Singleton Construction for Probabilistic Group Testing
papers.abstract: We consider the probabilistic nonadaptive group testing problem, in which a uniformly random defective set of size $d$ is to be identified among $N$ items using a binary test matrix. For the explicit Kautz--Singleton construction, it is known that order-optimal scaling $T=\Theta(d\log N)$ for high-probability recovery can be achieved in the regime $d=\Omega(\log^2 N)$. However, the leading constant in this scaling remains uncharacterized even for standard low-complexity decoders. In this work, we revisit the probabilistic analysis of this construction and improve the leading constant for the COMP decoder, as well as establishing the same bound for the DD decoder. Our approach relies on a sharper analysis of the number of distinct roots associated with the defective items, yielding tighter bounds on the decoding error probability. In particular, we show that both COMP and DD achieve vanishing average error probability with $T\le (1/\ln 2+\varepsilon)d\log N$ tests for any $\varepsilon>0$, in the admissible regime $N=q^k$ for some prime power $q = \Theta(d)$ and integer $k \ge 2$. For COMP, this leading constant matches that of the random near-constant column weight design, whereas for DD, a gap remains except in the sparse regime $d = N^{o(1)}$.

papers.title: Inference for Linear Systems with Unknown Coefficients
papers.abstract: This paper considers the problem of testing whether there exists a solution satisfying known linear constraints to a linear system of equations. Importantly and in contrast to some prior work, we allow all parameters in the system of equations, including the slope coefficients, to be unknown. For this reason, we describe the linear system as having unknown (as opposed to known) coefficients. This hypothesis testing problem arises naturally when constructing confidence sets for possibly partially identified parameters in the analysis of nonparametric instrumental variables models, treatment effect models, and random coefficient models, among other settings. We begin our analysis by providing a novel characterization of the set of coefficient pairs for which the linear system is feasible. Leveraging this characterization, we develop a testing procedure based on sample splitting. We establish its validity under weak and interpretable conditions on the linear system. An important feature of these conditions is that they permit the dimensionality of the problem to grow rapidly with the sample size. A further attractive property of our test is that it does not require simulation to compute suitable critical values. We illustrate the practical relevance of our theoretical results in a simulation study.

papers.title: The empirical discrete copula process
papers.abstract: This paper develops a general inferential framework for discrete copulas on finite supports in any dimension. The copula of a multivariate discrete distribution is defined as Csiszar's I-projection (i.e., the minimum-Kullback-Leibler divergence projection) of its joint probability array onto the polytope of uniform-margins probability arrays of the same size, and its empirical estimator is obtained by applying that same projection to the array of empirical frequencies observed on the sample. Under the assumption of random sampling, strong consistency and $\sqrt{n}$-asymptotic normality of the empirical copula array is established. The theory is illustrated by deriving the large-sample distribution of Yule's concordance coefficient (the natural analogue of Spearman's $\rho$ for bivariate discrete distributions) and by constructing a test for quasi-independence in multivariate contingency tables.

papers.title: Transferring supremum-norm rates and weak convergence of covariance kernel estimators to functional principal components
papers.abstract: We show that $L_2$-perturbation theory can be used to transfer rates of convergence in the supremum norm as well as weak convergence in the space of continuous functions from covariance kernel estimators to the associated functional \rev{principal} components. As an application we obtain optimal rates of convergence in sup-norm, including minimax-lower bounds, as well as asymptotic normality for estimating the functional principal components in a discrete observational model with errors under fixed, synchronous design. The sparse to dense transition which has previously been observed for mean function and covariance kernel estimators also applies here. Surprisingly, eigenvalue estimation exhibits a discretization-dominated regime under sparse designs, too. Our results further apply to estimators of cross-covariance and long-run covariance kernels, as well as to covariance kernels of derivative processes. We also present results of numerical experiments in which we use the Nystr\"om method to compute functional principal components and eigenvalues, and give an empirical illustration to series of daily temperature curves.

papers.title: Stopping models closed under pgf composition, and the stability of randomly stopped model extensions
papers.abstract: Statistical model transformations based on randomly stopped sums, maxima, and minima are widely used to extend statistical models by introducing an additional parameter. We characterize the finite-dimensional positive stopping models for which these randomly stopped sum and extreme transformations act as statistically stable (idempotent) model extensions. Stability requires the underlying stopping model to be closed under pgf composition. We prove that any finite-dimensional, connected, positive stopping model closed under pgf composition necessarily forms a family of random variables whose pgfs commute. Using the associated Koenigs function, we establish that these models form a statistical manifold admitting a global, one-dimensional parametrization $\theta = \Pr(N=1) \in (0, \theta_*]$, in which the probability mass at $i$ is a polynomial in $\theta$ of degree at most $i$. Within this class, we further establish a duality between those models containing the identity variable (the ones yielding statistically stable extensions) and the set of all probability distributions supported on the positive integers. By providing numerous examples of stopping models closed under pgf composition, we clarify the assertion that, under certain conditions, the only stopping model that is so is geometric.

papers.title: Error analysis and optimal sample allocation for randomized unbiased estimation: the single term estimator
papers.abstract: Randomized unbiased estimation can be highly efficient for approximating expectations of functionals of stochastic differential equations. However, in practice, the optimal computational efficiency is rarely attained due to errors arising from parameter estimation and truncation. The effects of these errors on computational efficiency have not been investigated. In this article, we study the error analysis and optimal sample allocation for the single term estimator. Specifically, under mild assumptions on the estimated parameters, we develop a unified error analysis that incorporates both sources of error, and establish the relevant convergence rates for the computational efficiency loss. Based on this analysis, we further investigate the optimal allocation of the computational budget for parameter estimation, and propose several efficient sample allocation strategies. Numerical experiments support the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

papers.title: Gaussian-efficient nonasymptotic confidence sets for unbounded means
papers.abstract: Consider the classical statistical problem of sub-Gaussian mean estimation under martingale dependence: given $n$ observations with conditional mean $\mu$ and a known conditional sub-Gaussian proxy $s>0$, we seek a nonasymptotically valid confidence interval for $\mu$. The usual Chernoff interval has half-width $s\sqrt{2\log(2/\alpha)/n}$; it neither adapts to the actual standard deviation $\sigma\le s$ nor attains the Gaussian quantile $z_{1-\alpha/2}$. We construct an analytically closed-form nonasymptotically-valid interval under martingale dependence whose endpoints, at every iid law with $\sigma > 0$, agree almost surely to first order with $\bar X_n\pm\sigma z_{1-\alpha/2}/\sqrt n$. The two new building blocks are a sub-Gaussian exponential supermartingale with an \emph{empirical} quadratic variance and a cubic correction term, and a sub-Gaussian continuation supermartingale, the former delivering variance adaptivity ("Empirical-Bernstein'' for unbounded data), the latter also providing the Gaussian quantile ("Empirical-Berry-Esseen'' for unbounded data). The same constructions yield a closed-form time-uniform confidence sequence with asymptotically unimprovable half-width $\sigma\sqrt{2\log\log n/n}$. We also give closed-form multivariate ellipsoids with the true-covariance chi-square limit, and extend the scalar Gaussian and LIL constructions to handle heavy-tailed settings where one only knows a bound on any absolute central moment of order greater than two. Experiments show substantial width reductions when the true variance is smaller than the implied variance bound, at small loss in the boundary cases. The surprising (to us) takeaway message is: given any more than two moments, one can construct fully data dependent nonasymptotic confidence sets for the mean that are asymptotically efficient.

papers.title: Inference in High-Dimensional Linear Mediation Models
papers.abstract: Mediation analysis plays an important role in psychology, epidemiology, and genomics. Al- though high-dimensional mediation has been studied extensively, existing inferential methods typically rely on sparsity assumptions that may be difficult to justify when many individually weak mediators collectively produce a substantial effect. We study inference for both the over- all indirect effect and the effect transmitted through an individual mediator in a proportional high-dimensional regime, where the number of mediators and the sample size grow at compa- rable rates, without imposing sparsity on the mediator effects. Standard debiasing procedures for high-dimensional inference commonly rely on design-covariance information or additional structural assumptions on precision-matrix directions. In mediation models, however, the full outcome-design covariance depends on unknown mediator-model coefficients, creating an addi- tional challenge when such information or structure is unavailable. To address this challenge, we introduce an approximate debiasing procedure based on partial ridge regression and show that the resulting estimator is asymptotically bias-corrected and Gaussian. We also develop a cross-fitted estimator with a smaller asymptotic variance than its sample-split counterpart. In addition, we construct consistent estimators of the limiting variances of both the sample-split and cross-fitted estimators. Together, these results provide feasible inferential procedures for global and pathwise mediation effects.
